title: Potato Physical Chemistry & Biophysics — Water, Starch, Ions, Pressure, Heat and Fields
purpose: Explain potato behavior using measurable physical chemistry: water chemical potential, osmotic/turgor pressure, semi-crystalline starch, ion binding, diffusion, gas transport, mechanics, thermal transitions, dielectric response and electrochemistry.
epistemic_boundary: These are ordinary physical and chemical processes. They provide grounded comparators for project language such as storage, pressure, flow, boundary and release, but they do not imply a new fundamental force.

composition_as_material.bulk: Fresh potato tubers are typically about 80% water and about 20% dry matter, with starch the dominant dry-matter component; exact composition is cultivar- and condition-dependent.
composition_as_material.material_view: The tuber is a water-rich, porous, pressurized cellular composite containing polymer-rich cell walls, ion-containing aqueous phases and semi-crystalline starch granules.
composition_as_material.consequence: Its macroscopic behavior emerges from coupled water, polymer, membrane, cell-wall and granular-starch physics rather than from starch alone.

water_and_chemical_potential.osmotic_principle: Water moves in response to water-potential/chemical-potential differences across semipermeable membranes and porous tissues.
water_and_chemical_potential.turgor: Cellular osmotic water uptake generates hydrostatic turgor pressure that pre-stresses cell walls and contributes strongly to raw-tuber firmness.
water_and_chemical_potential.loss_of_turgor: Water loss, membrane damage or thermal loss of semipermeability reduces turgor and changes mechanical response.
model_examples: van't Hoff ideal osmotic comparator: Π ≈ i C R T for dilute solutions
water-potential bookkeeping: Ψ = Ψ_s + Ψ_p + Ψ_g + Ψ_m, with relevant terms depending on scale
diffusive transport: J = -D ∇c as a first approximation
water_and_chemical_potential.caution: Plant tissues are non-ideal, heterogeneous and multicompartmental; these equations are local approximations, not whole-tuber exact laws.

molecular_components.amylose: Mostly linear alpha-glucan fraction, commonly about 20–33% of potato starch depending on cultivar/source.
molecular_components.amylopectin: Highly branched alpha-glucan forming most of the semi-crystalline granule structure.
molecular_components.phosphate: Potato amylopectin carries relatively abundant covalently bound phosphate monoesters, especially at C-6 and C-3 positions, contributing to hydration, ion interactions, swelling and viscosity.
molecular_components.lipids: Native potato starch contains very little endogenous lipid compared with many cereal starches.

granule_structure.size: Potato starch granules are unusually large, often spanning roughly 10–100 micrometres depending on source and fraction.
granule_structure.crystallinity: Native potato starch commonly shows B-type crystallinity with alternating amorphous and semi-crystalline lamellae.
granule_structure.birefringence: Ordered radial/semi-crystalline structure produces birefringence under crossed polarizers; gelatinization destroys this ordered optical signature.
granule_structure.internal_water: NMR work resolves multiple water populations inside native potato starch, including water associated with amorphous and semi-crystalline regions and channel water in B-type crystalline structure.

gelatinization_phase_transition.typical_range: Cultivar-dependent potato starch gelatinization commonly begins around the high-50s to low-60s °C, peaks around low- to mid-60s °C and concludes around upper-60s to low-70s °C in high-moisture conditions.
gelatinization_phase_transition.thermodynamics: Differential scanning calorimetry measures onset, peak, conclusion and gelatinization enthalpy; representative cultivar studies report enthalpies around 15–18 J/g.
gelatinization_phase_transition.project_value: This is a literal, measurable phase transition from ordered granular polymer structure to a hydrated, swollen, viscoelastic state.

starch_as_soft_matter.retrogradation: On cooling/storage, gelatinized starch chains can reassociate into more ordered structures; extent depends on amylose/amylopectin architecture, water and thermal history.

rheology.behavior: Gelatinized potato starch forms high-viscosity, viscoelastic pastes and gels.
rheology.cause: Granule swelling, polymer entanglement, amylose/amylopectin architecture, phosphate groups, water and shear history jointly determine flow.

cell_wall_and_mechanics.raw_tissue: Raw potato texture is produced by pressurized cells whose walls and middle lamella carry and redistribute mechanical stress.
cell_wall_and_mechanics.anisotropy: Potato parenchyma exhibits direction-dependent mechanical response; anisotropy and stiffness change with turgor and storage history.
cooking_transition: starch granules absorb water and swell
membrane semipermeability is lost and turgor falls
pectin chemistry changes and intercellular adhesion weakens
fracture mode shifts toward cell separation rather than cell rupture
cell_wall_and_mechanics.calcium_pectin: Ca2+ can ionically crosslink de-esterified pectin domains and strengthen intercellular adhesion; pulsed-electric-field or mild-thermal treatments can alter pectin methylesterification and calcium binding.
cell_wall_and_mechanics.acid_effect: Acidic pretreatment can remodel pectin chemistry and its interaction with cellulose, changing cooked texture.
cell_wall_and_mechanics.micromechanics: Single-cell compression experiments show cultivar- and heat-dependent force–deformation behavior and bursting events.

heat_and_mass_transfer.heat_equation: ρ c_p ∂T/∂t = ∇·(k ∇T) + q_dot is a standard local heat-transfer model, with temperature- and composition-dependent material properties.
heat_and_mass_transfer.thermal_diffusivity: Experimental potato values are of order 10^-7 m^2/s; one classic study reported about 1.3–1.4 × 10^-7 m^2/s for a fresh potato cultivar.
heat_and_mass_transfer.thermal_conductivity: Thermal conductivity depends strongly on moisture content and tends to fall as potato tissue dries.
heat_and_mass_transfer.drying: Drying couples heat transfer, water diffusion, shrinkage/structural change and evolving porosity; effective moisture diffusivity and surface-transfer coefficients are process-dependent.
heat_and_mass_transfer.frying: Frying couples rapid heat input to water evaporation, steam formation, moisture diffusion, crust formation and oil uptake; effective moisture diffusivity rises strongly with frying temperature.
heat_and_mass_transfer.project_value: The tuber is a coupled heat-and-mass-transfer object, so 'release' is physically better modeled as flux through gradients than as a single stored quantity suddenly vanishing.

gas_transport.pathway: O2 entry and CO2 exit occur primarily through lenticels, then through internal air spaces and tissue diffusion.
gas_transport.permeability: Mature periderm without lenticels is far less permeable to gases than lenticel regions.
gas_transport.internal_porosity: Intercellular air space is only a small fraction of tuber volume but provides a fast gas-phase route because gas diffusivity in air is orders of magnitude greater than in water.
gas_transport.storage_consequence: Lenticel state, temperature, respiration rate and atmosphere determine internal gas conditions and can influence dormancy, sprouting and hypoxia risk.
gas_transport.simple_model: J_gas = -D_eff ∇c with D_eff determined by gas/water pathways, porosity, tortuosity and boundary permeability.

electrical_and_dielectric_physics.ionic_conduction: Potato tissue contains water and dissolved ions, so it supports ionic conduction rather than metallic electronic conduction.
electrical_and_dielectric_physics.dielectric_response: Alternating electric fields polarize membranes, ions and water; dielectric spectroscopy can therefore sense tissue composition and dry matter.
electrical_and_dielectric_physics.impedance_model: Living tissue can be approximated by equivalent circuits with extracellular resistance, membrane capacitance and intracellular resistance; drying, heating or membrane damage shifts the spectrum.
electrical_and_dielectric_physics.electroporation: Pulsed electric fields can raise transmembrane voltage enough to create transient or permanent pores in cell membranes, changing permeability and texture without requiring bulk cooking.
electrical_and_dielectric_physics.food_processing_use: PEF is studied as a way to alter potato cell permeability, facilitate cutting/extraction and tune subsequent texture.
electrical_and_dielectric_physics.project_value: A potato has real field-dependent behavior, but it is ordinary dielectric polarization, ionic current and membrane electroporation—not an exotic Potato field.

electrochemistry_and_potato_battery.correction: The potato is not the fuel in the familiar zinc/copper 'potato battery'.
electrochemistry_and_potato_battery.mechanism: Two dissimilar metal electrodes supply the redox couple; the potato's water, salts and acids act mainly as an electrolyte supporting ionic charge transport.
electrochemistry_and_potato_battery.circuit: electrode oxidation/reduction + external electron flow + internal ionic current
electrochemistry_and_potato_battery.project_value: This is a clean example of medium versus source: the tuber can enable charge transport without being the origin of the electrode free energy.

chemical_reactivity_and_processing.amino_acid_interest: Asparagine is especially important in fried-potato chemistry.
chemical_reactivity_and_processing.maillard: At high processing temperatures, reducing sugars react with amino compounds through Maillard chemistry, generating color/flavor compounds and potentially acrylamide from asparagine-rich systems.
chemical_reactivity_and_processing.cold_storage_link: Cold-induced sweetening raises reducing sugars, connecting storage temperature directly to later frying chemistry.
chemical_reactivity_and_processing.glycoalkaloid_rule: Light/stress can accompany greening and glycoalkaloid changes; chlorophyll itself is not the toxic principle.
chemical_reactivity_and_processing.redox: Potato tissue maintains measurable redox state and pH; wound, stress and metabolism alter ROS/antioxidant chemistry.

useful_formalisms.name: chemical free-energy flow
useful_formalisms.use: frame storage/release reactions thermodynamically rather than as a new force

useful_formalisms.name: diffusion
useful_formalisms.use: water, solute and gas transport approximation

useful_formalisms.name: Darcy/porous flow comparator
useful_formalisms.use: pressure-driven flow only where porous-continuum assumptions are justified

useful_formalisms.name: Arrhenius kinetics
useful_formalisms.use: temperature-dependent reactions and effective transport models where empirically justified
